text: Stevens permit himself the space to openly reflect upon his feelings for Miss Kenton. As he says, if a butler is to be ‘great’, then the only time that he lays his professionalism to one side is when he is completely alone; Stevens is aware of the presence of his reader and so never strays from fully inhabiting his role. Because of this, we must read into the implications of Stevens’ words and actions. He coats his flirtation with Miss Kenton in the guise of professionalism, for example their “cocoa evenings”, in which they would begin discussing work matters before drifting into more “harmless” trivial ones, “which did much, one should say, to relieve the many tensions produced by a hard day” (p. 157). More than simply “relieving the tensions of a hard day”, Stevens is communicating that he enjoys passing a relaxed time in her presence; it is something that makes him happy. The reader must decipher such comments because Stevens only speaks in terms of how something affects his work, and never in terms of how it makes him happy or unhappy. Like all humans, Stevens is an emotional being, but because of the extremely high professional standards he sets himself he has no outlet for emotional expression. As a result, we can only detect it surfacing in specific infrequent moments, such as when Stevens is caught reading a sentimental love story. He is clearly embarrassed when Miss Kenton intrudes into his study and demands to know what he is reading, because he is reluctant to show her the book’s title. When he eventually reveals that he is a reading a sentimental romance he rationalises it with reference to his work, saying that it improves his spoken command of the English language, a quality that all great butlers must possess. Just as Stevens justifies his cocoa evenings with Miss Kenton by affirming that they are essential to the proper running of the household, and his trip to Cornwall by claiming that it is to remedy the understaffing problem at Darlington Hall, he justifies reading the romance novel in relation to his profession. In other words, Stevens supresses his emotions by subordinating them to the professional needs of his work. FURTHER REFLECTION SOME QUESTIONS TO THINK ABOUT… At the end of the novel Stevens has a conversation with a stranger on a bench who makes reference to the title by encouraging Stevens to enjoy the remainder of his day given that he has “done his day’s work” (p. 244). Why do you think Ishiguro includes this brief conversation at the close of the novel? Do you think Stevens is likely to heed the stranger’s advice? Could Ishiguro have set this novel in any time and place? What is the significance of the particular historical context in furthering the novel’s themes and message? To what extent do you agree that Stevens is a reliable narrative voice, and that we can trust his reporting of the events of the story? One of the themes that appears in many of Ishiguro’s works is the inevitability of human failure and shortcoming. Is this applicable to The Remains of the Day ? Why/why not? Due to the fact that Stevens’ professional standards and expectations are so high, he often makes comments that to us seem comically exaggerated, such as when he compares the butler’s pantry to “general’s headquarters during a battle” (p. 165). How is Stevens’ narration an effective way to insert humour into the novel? When Miss Kenton and Stevens finally meet at the end of the novel, Stevens remarks “Well, whatever awaits me, Mrs Benn, I know I’m not awaited by emptiness. If only I were. But oh no, there’s work, work and more work” (p. 237). Discuss how Ishiguro creates this contrast between what the reader sees as empty and Stevens sees as meaningful. If you were to ask Stevens what the meaning of life was, what might he respond given what we know about his character? Throughout the novel, Stevens reflects on the ‘greatness’ of England, claiming that the stoicism and composure of an English butler is simply unrivalled. In your opinion, is Ishiguro celebrating this supposed ‘greatness’ or criticising it? Explain your answer. In 1928 all women and men over the age of 21 were granted the right to vote, resulting in universal suffrage. How does the question of the ordinary citizen’s role in national affairs surface in Ishiguro’s text? FURTHER READING REFERENCE EDITION Ishiguro, K. (1989) The Remains of the Day. New York: Alfred A.
